text.title: Freelance Proposal Template Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for freelance-proposal-template. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Proposal MUST contain a scope envelope: WHAT IS INCLUDED, WHAT IS EXCLUDED. Exclusions section is mandatory; absent exclusions is a forbidden pattern.
rule.rationale: Inclusions alone leave the boundary implicit, and the two sides fill the gap with different defaults: the client assumes the obvious adjacent work is covered, the contractor assumes it was never quoted. Written exclusions move that argument to before signature, where it is a scope conversation, instead of mid-project, where it is a dispute about money already committed.

rule.statement: Each assumption the bid depends on MUST be listed with a confirm-by date; un-confirmed assumptions auto-trigger renegotiation.
rule.rationale: A bid is a price computed from unverified beliefs about access, decision speed and existing systems. Left implicit, a false assumption surfaces mid-delivery and its cost is silently absorbed by the contractor, who has no contractual hook to reopen the price. A confirm-by date makes verification someone's job and creates the trigger that reopens the number before the work is sunk.

rule.statement: Payment is broken into at least three milestones; final milestone is at most 30% of total to align incentives.
rule.rationale: A solo contractor with no billing between kickoff and delivery is financing the client's project out of personal cash flow and carries the entire non-payment risk in one lump. The cap matters at the other end: when too much money rides on the final payment, acceptance becomes leverage, and the client can extract unbilled extra work simply by not signing off.

rule.statement: Proposal pins a change-request hourly rate (usually 1.5× base rate) and a minimum block (often 1 hour); scope-creep is priced, not absorbed.
rule.rationale: With no priced path for changes, every request is a yes-or-fight choice, and a contractor who wants the relationship says yes. A published rate supplies a third answer, that this is N hours, which lets the client decide whether the change is worth buying. Pricing it above base is what stops change requests becoming the cheapest route to work that belonged in the original scope, and the minimum block stops death by ten-minute favours.

rule.statement: Late payment beyond NET-30 incurs interest at a stated rate; work pauses at NET-45.
rule.rationale: Payment terms with no consequence are a request. The clause earns its place less as interest income than by making the chase a contractual step instead of an awkward personal message. The pre-agreed pause is the only leverage a solo contractor has, because delivered work cannot be un-delivered, so the stop has to come before the next tranche of it.

rule.statement: IP transfers to the client only upon final payment; pre-payment, all work remains the BA's IP.
rule.rationale: Once deliverables are handed over, an unpaid contractor's only remaining leverage is legal action disproportionate to the invoice. Conditioning transfer on final payment means a client who withholds payment is holding files it cannot lawfully put into production, which turns a slow debt-collection problem into an immediate operational one for the party who can actually resolve it.

rule.statement: Proposal expires in 14 days; after that, terms (rate, availability) may change without notice.
rule.rationale: An open-ended proposal is a free option: the client can hold the quoted rate and reserved availability while shopping, then return months later expecting both to stand. An expiry prices that option at zero and supplies the one follow-up reason that is not a nudge, namely the deadline itself. It also protects a quote built on a schedule that no longer exists.

rule.statement: If you are not bidding fixed-scope freelance work, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: Every clause here is machinery for defending a fixed number against changing scope. On open-scope hourly work there is no number to defend, since scope changes are already priced by the clock, so exclusions, milestones and a change-request rate only add friction to a negotiation that carries none of the risk they exist to control.
